passages.expected_base: Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.
passages.text: The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask me, a Samaritan woman, for a drink?” For Jews do not ask Samaritans for help.
passages.rationale:
Why is Jesus' request for water surprising?
Manning proposes «seek help from» to explain the woman's reaction, rather than «associate with» or «share vessels with».

Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. The traditional explanation, «Jews have no dealings with Samaritans», sounds like a prohibition of all social contact. Another interpretation concerns sharing vessels and ritual purity. The question turns on synchraomai, a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament.

Manning examines its use elsewhere in Greek. With a person or group as its object, he finds the sense of obtaining assistance: Polybius, for example, uses it for support from fleets and allied forces. «Samaritans» is a dative object; the proposed sense «use something together with Samaritans» requires a grammatical relationship that the parallels do not support. Splitting the verb into its components does not establish its meaning either.

On this reading, the woman's surprise is that a Jew would seek a Samaritan's help. It fits Jesus' immediate request for water. Manning acknowledges some ancient support for the traditional interpretation; his proposal rests on usage and context, rather than on unanimous scholarly agreement.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jews do not “associate with” Samaritans? Or do not “share vessels with” Samaritans? Or something else? (John 4:9) · 2025-07-30

passages.expected_base: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
passages.text: For God loved the world so much that he gave his only begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.
passages.rationale:
«So loved»: both the manner and the extent of love
The gift of the Son shows how God loves and how far that love reaches.

Some translations say «God loved the world in this way», while others emphasize «God loved the world so much». The first is sometimes presented as a necessary correction: the verse supposedly describes manner but never intensity. Manning argues that this opposition overlooks the complete construction.

Houtōs can mean «in this way». Here, however, it combines with hōste to introduce a result: God loved so that he gave his Son. The combination can express degree or extent as well as manner. Manning compares Acts 14:1 and examples from Josephus and other Greek writers, where restricting the expression to manner does not adequately explain the stated result.

The gift of the Son therefore supplies both the concrete expression and the measure of God's love. The KJV's «so loved» need not be replaced on the assumption that intensity is impossible. Nor should it become a vague statement of emotion, detached from the saving gift described in the rest of the sentence.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · “God so loved” or “God loved in this way”? · 2025-05-05
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2025/god-so-loved-or-god-loved-in-this-way
passages.editorial_audit: Manning argues that houtos with hoste can express degree, not exclusively manner. KJV already conveys the intensity of love. The draft retains only begotten rather than deciding the separate monogenes question without further research.

passages.expected_base: But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God.
passages.text: But whoever practices the truth comes to the light, so that others may see that their deeds have been done in God.
passages.rationale:
To whom are the works made visible?
Coming to the light makes a life wrought in God visible to others, rather than informing an unaware God.

John 3:19–21 contrasts people who avoid the light to conceal their conduct with those who come into it. The KJV's «that his deeds may be made manifest» does not name the observers. Readers may imagine that the deeds are being revealed to God, as though he needed to discover them.

Manning examines phaneroō, the verb for making something manifest. Elsewhere in John it concerns disclosure to human beings: Jesus manifests his glory at Cana (2:11), public manifestation is discussed in 7:4, and the risen Jesus manifests himself to his disciples in 21:1. This pattern favors a human audience here too.

Rendering the passive as «so that others can see» can therefore clarify a relationship left implicit in English. It does not arbitrarily invent a different audience. What becomes visible is not personal goodness independent of God: the closing words identify the deeds as wrought in God. The contrast concerns concealing evil or allowing God's work to be recognized.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Revealed to Whom? (John 3:21) · 2011-07-18
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2011/revealed-to-whom-john-3-21

passages.expected_base: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
passages.text: When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
passages.rationale:
«It is finished»: the mission reaches completion
The popular «paid in full» explanation confuses Jesus' word with a different expression on ancient tax receipts.

It is often claimed that tetelestai was stamped on receipts to mean «paid in full», so Jesus was announcing payment of sin's debt. Manning reexamines the documents behind that claim. Around 315 Egyptian customs receipts contain the abbreviation tetel. In 17, the unabbreviated form identifies it as tetelōnētai, «paid as taxes», rather than the word used in John 19:30.

Teleō can concern payment where taxes are specified, but this does not establish tetelestai as a banking formula. John's own context is the completion of the Father's work (4:34; 5:36; 17:4). In 19:28–30, that completion is also linked with the fulfillment of Scripture.

The KJV's «It is finished» accordingly announces the culmination of Jesus' mission through the cross. Theological explanations involving a debt may draw on other passages; they should not be inserted here as though «paid in full» were the demonstrated historical meaning of Jesus' final word.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · “Paid in Full”? The Meaning of τετέλεσται (Tetelestai) in Jesus’ Final Words · 2022-04-20
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2022/paid-in-full-the-meaning-of-tetelestai-in-jesus-final-words
passages.editorial_audit: Tetelestai expresses completion, linked with 19:28. KJV's It is finished is retained. Paid in full imports a debt absent from the clause; atonement belongs in interpretation rather than a forced lexical substitution.

passages.expected_base: After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst.
passages.rationale:
Thirst within a mission reaching fulfillment
The repeated language of completion prepares the meaning of «It is finished» in verse 30.

Before mentioning Jesus' thirst, John says that he knows all things are accomplished. His words are then related to the fulfillment of Scripture. After receiving the sour wine, he declares «It is finished» and dies. This sequence places the final declaration within the narrative, rather than leaving its meaning dependent on an alleged commercial custom.

Manning notes the neighboring verbs teleō, «finish», and teleioō, «bring to completion», in 19:28–30. They recall the Father's work entrusted to Jesus in 4:34 and 5:36 and the completion described in his prayer in 17:4. The cross brings this mission to its culmination, together with the scriptural fulfillment emphasized by John.

Verse 30 should therefore be read through this preparation. Jesus' thirst remains a bodily reality while also occupying a meaningful place in the fulfillment sequence. Neither the thirst nor tetelestai needs to become a financial code to explain the passage's significance.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · “Paid in Full”? The Meaning of τετέλεσται (Tetelestai) in Jesus’ Final Words · 2022-04-20
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2022/paid-in-full-the-meaning-of-tetelestai-in-jesus-final-words

passages.expected_base: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
passages.text: Indeed, I consider everything a loss compared with the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For him I have lost everything and consider it rubbish, so that I may gain Christ.
passages.rationale:
Loss and gain, rather than an alleged swear word
Paul compares his former credentials to waste in order to express the surpassing value of knowing Christ.

Skybala can denote rubbish, discarded material or dung. This has prompted claims that Paul used a particularly offensive swear word. Manning distinguishes a word's unpleasant referent from its social register: referring to excrement does not automatically amount to swearing.

In the Greek evidence he surveys, doctors, historians and philosophers use skybala without indications of vulgarity. Papyri add an economic setting: the word describes crop waste, spoiled hay and low-value remains that might be sold cheaply or recorded as a loss. Such uses fit Philippians 3:7–8, with its repeated language of gain, loss and gaining Christ.

Paul is reassessing his own religious advantages, listed in 3:4–6, as grounds for confidence. Beside knowing Christ, former assets belong among things to be discarded. The KJV's «dung» conveys one possible strong image; «waste» conveys the comparison without making Paul use an obscenity that Manning's evidence does not establish.

passages.expected_base: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
passages.text: The eye is the lamp of the body. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light.
passages.rationale:
The «single eye» and the use of money
Manning reads the image as generosity, drawing on Jewish idioms and Matthew's surrounding teaching.

What does an eye have to do with a life full of light? The saying stands between instructions about treasure (6:19–21) and the choice between serving God and serving wealth (6:24). Manning argues that this setting directs the image toward the use of possessions.

The «evil eye» denotes stinginess or envy in Deuteronomy 15:9 and Matthew 20:15. Conversely, Proverbs 22:9 connects a «good eye» with sharing food with the poor. Words related to haplous, the adjective translated «single» in the KJV, express generosity in Romans 12:8 and 2 Corinthians 9:11. Together these parallels support a reading in which generosity brings light to the whole life.

Other interpreters favor a healthy or sincere eye, and Luke 11 places the parallel saying in a different immediate setting. Generosity is therefore an argued interpretation, rather than the undisputed meaning of every word. Preserving the image alongside its explanation makes both the evidence and the interpretive choice visible.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Good Eye / Bad Eye · 2011-02-04

passages.expected_base: But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!
passages.text: But if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. If the light within you is darkness, how great that darkness is!
passages.rationale:
The «evil eye»: greed that darkens a life
The image concerns a stingy disposition, rather than defective eyesight or a magically harmful glance.

This verse continues the contrast with the good eye and precedes the impossibility of serving both God and wealth (6:24). Manning connects it with a Jewish idiom: an «evil eye» looks on possessions with greed or resents sharing them.

Deuteronomy 15:9 warns against withholding help from the poor for a self-interested financial reason. Proverbs 23:6 and 28:22 connect such an eye with stinginess, and Matthew 20:15 uses the image when workers resent the landowner's generosity. The point is not that physically unhealthy eyes create spiritual wickedness.

Darkness describes the reach of this disposition: attachment to money shapes the whole life and its ultimate allegiance. Manning notes that a paraphrase can capture greed in the evil eye while missing generosity in the preceding contrast. The two verses belong together; their imagery should remain connected to possessions and the choice of serving God.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Good Eye / Bad Eye · 2011-02-04

passages.expected_base: Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
passages.text: Am I not free to do what I wish with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?
passages.rationale:
An «evil eye» at the owner's goodness
The workers complain when they compare their pay with generosity shown to others.

Those hired first receive the wage they agreed to, yet resent the equal payment given to latecomers. The owner has not reduced their promised wages. Their objection arises when they see the favorable treatment of others. His closing question contrasts their «evil eye» with his own goodness.

Manning uses this scene to explain the eye idiom. It concerns envy or stinginess in response to generosity, rather than a problem with physical sight. The situation supplies the meaning without requiring readers to derive it from isolated words. It also helps illuminate the good and evil eyes in Matthew 6:22–23.

The parable challenges a perspective that evaluates goodness by one's comparative advantage. It does not establish that every employer's economic decision is automatically just: in this story, the agreed wage is paid and the dispute concerns benefits given to others. That distinction keeps the application anchored in Jesus' actual scene.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Good Eye / Bad Eye · 2011-02-04

passages.expected_base: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
passages.text: She gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the guest room.
passages.rationale:
A manger does not require an innkeeper
The lodging term can refer to guest accommodation; several familiar nativity details are later reconstructions.

The familiar scene includes an innkeeper refusing the couple on the night they arrive and a separate stable. Luke mentions a manger but supplies neither that character nor that sequence. He says Mary gave birth while they were in Bethlehem (2:6), without identifying the birth with their arrival night.

Manning points out that katalyma, translated «inn» in the KJV, denotes a guest room in Luke 22:11. He proposes a lack of space in family accommodation. Feeding troughs could occupy domestic areas used for animals, so a manger alone does not prove a separate building. The precise arrangement remains a plausible reconstruction, rather than a fully described detail in Luke.

Swaddling clothes are not burial wrappings either: the Greek terminology describes ordinary care of newborns. This distinction separates the narrative from later imagination. Its striking humility remains: the child announced as Savior is placed in a feeding trough, without requiring additional details to heighten the scene.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · What are Swaddling Clothes? · 2021-12-20

passages.expected_base: And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
passages.rationale:
Ordinary swaddling, an unexpected bed
The sign identifies a newborn lying in a manger, rather than special cloths for sacrificial lambs or corpses.

The old-fashioned phrase «swaddling clothes» can invite explanations that Mary used burial wrappings or cloths intended for sacrificial lambs. Manning investigates the Greek vocabulary for swaddling babies, sparganoō and sparganon, in literature before and after the New Testament. He finds an ordinary practice, rather than an exceptional ritual garment.

Writers such as Galen and Plutarch associate these cloths with birth, warmth and infant care. Expressions meaning «from swaddling clothes» can even stand for «from infancy». The angels' description therefore first tells the shepherds that they are looking for a newborn.

The manger supplies the distinctive location: a feeding trough has become the baby's bed. Together the details identify the child. Their significance does not require a symbolism built on an alleged funerary or sacrificial meaning that the vocabulary's actual use does not demonstrate.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · What are Swaddling Clothes? · 2021-12-20

passages.expected_base: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
passages.text: Make every effort to present yourself to God as approved, a worker who has no cause for shame and who teaches the word of truth rightly.
passages.rationale:
Keeping the teaching on a straight course
Faithfulness to the word involves avoiding pointless detours as well as teaching accurately.

The KJV's «rightly dividing the word of truth» renders orthotomeō, a metaphor associated with cutting straight. It can suggest accurate workmanship or making a straight path without deviation. Manning favors the latter emphasis without denying the importance of accuracy.

He offers two reasons. The Greek translation of Proverbs 3:6 and 11:5 uses the verb for straightening paths. The surrounding passage also warns against wrangling over words (2:14), empty chatter (2:16) and foolish disputes (2:23). A straight path aptly describes teaching that does not leave its purpose to follow these distractions.

The approved worker is therefore not instructed to partition Scripture mechanically or accumulate impressive details. Teaching should remain directed toward edifying truth, avoiding both error and unproductive speculation. This is an argument about the metaphor's emphasis, rather than an undisputed definition that can be imposed wherever the verb occurs.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Handling Accurately or Teaching Straight? · 2010-03-12
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2010/03/handling-accurately-or-teaching.html

passages.expected_base: But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
passages.text: Instead, speaking the truth in love, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ.
passages.rationale:
Teaching truth so the church grows together
The main contrast is between deceptive teaching and truth communicated in love to the community.

«Speaking the truth in love» is often quoted to recommend tact when correcting someone in a personal conflict. Manning accepts that advice but observes that this paragraph concerns the growth of the whole church. Believers are to stop being children carried about by every teaching and mature into Christ (4:13–16).

Alētheuontes can mean «speaking truth». Its immediate opposite here is not merely rudeness or insincerity, but the doctrinal deception of verse 14. In Galatians 4:16, Paul's other use of the verb likewise concerns truth he communicates to his hearers. These considerations lead Manning to emphasize loving instruction in the truth.

The application is therefore larger than winning arguments or delivering unpleasant remarks politely. It concerns helping the community know and live the truth that unites it to Christ, its head. Other translations stress «practicing truth»; Manning's preference rests particularly on this paragraph's contrast and purpose.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Speaking the Truth in Love (Ephesians 4:15) · 2010-06-24

passages.expected_base: So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.
passages.rationale:
Peter's love is not measured by two Greek categories
His restoration emerges from the conversation and the shepherding commission, rather than a hierarchy between agapaō and phileō.

A familiar explanation says Jesus requests divine, unconditional love with agapaō while Peter offers only friendly affection with phileō. Manning objects that the verbs do not have those fixed categories. John uses both for love of the same Lazarus (11:3,5), and phileō also describes the Father's love for the Son (5:20).

Peter answers «yes»: he does not reject Jesus' requested kind of love and substitute an inferior one. The conversation also alternates words for knowing, feeding and tending, while the chapter varies words for fish and boats. Each lexical change need not encode a theological contrast.

The emphasis is that the disciple who denied Jesus now affirms his love and is entrusted with care for Jesus' flock. The repeated question recalls the three denials. Love becomes renewed service, rather than an examination of emotional levels supposedly hidden in synonyms.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Make Me a Higher Love? (agape/phileo) · 2008-09-08

passages.expected_base: He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
passages.rationale:
«Shepherd my sheep»: love receives a task
The second question sustains the connection between loving Jesus and accepting responsibility for others.

Jesus asks again and Peter again answers affirmatively. The alternation between agapaō in the question and phileō in the answer has been read as negotiation: Jesus asks for higher love while Peter offers something less. Manning notes that John uses both verbs for elevated relationships of love without establishing that hierarchy here.

The commission varies too: feeding alternates with tending, and lambs with sheep. These are related expressions within one responsibility, rather than separate flocks assigned to different grades of affection. Repetition strengthens Peter's commission and prepares the third question.

John 10 supplies the background of the shepherd who knows the flock and lays down his life for it. For Manning, restoration does not end in private assurance of forgiveness: Jesus calls the disciple back into self-giving service. Peter's following must take shape in caring for those who belong to Jesus, rather than proving superiority over other disciples.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Make Me a Higher Love? (agape/phileo) · 2008-09-08

passages.expected_base: He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
passages.rationale:
Why the third question grieves Peter
John attributes his grief to being asked a third time, rather than to a downgrade in the verb for love.

Jesus now uses phileō after using agapaō twice. A popular reading supposes that Peter is hurt because Jesus finally descends to Peter's inferior kind of love. Manning emphasizes the reason the narrator actually gives: Peter grieves because Jesus asks «the third time».

John treats the questions as repetitions of the same issue despite the alternating verbs. Peter appeals to Jesus' knowledge, himself varying the words for knowing. The narrative does not explain his pain through a technical distinction between two grades of affection.

The three affirmations correspond to the three denials in John 18. Beside a fire recalling that earlier night, Peter can publicly affirm what he previously denied and receives another commission to feed the flock. Manning locates the scene's force here: failure is confronted and service renewed. The following verses make clear that discipleship will eventually involve the cost of Peter's own life (21:18–19).

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Make Me a Higher Love? (agape/phileo) · 2008-09-08

John attributes his grief to being asked a third time, rather than to a downgrade in the verb for love.

Jesus now uses phileō after using agapaō twice. A popular reading supposes that Peter is hurt because Jesus finally descends to Peter's inferior kind of love. Manning emphasizes the reason the narrator actually gives: Peter grieves because Jesus asks «the third time».

John treats the questions as repetitions of the same issue despite the alternating verbs. Peter appeals to Jesus' knowledge, himself varying the words for knowing. The narrative does not explain his pain through a technical distinction between two grades of affection.

The three affirmations correspond to the three denials in John 18. Beside a fire recalling that earlier night, Peter can publicly affirm what he previously denied and receives another commission to feed the flock. Manning locates the scene's force here: failure is confronted and service renewed. The following verses make clear that discipleship will eventually involve the cost of Peter's own life (21:18–19).

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Make Me a Higher Love? (agape/phileo) · 2008-09-08

passages.expected_base: As soon then as they were come to land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.
passages.rationale:
A fire that brings Peter back to his denial
The charcoal detail connects breakfast with the night when the disciple denied knowing Jesus.

The disciples reach shore and find fish and bread over a charcoal fire. John also uses anthrakia in 18:18, where Peter warms himself while denying his relationship with Jesus. Manning draws attention to this correspondence as preparation for the conversation in 21:15–17.

The connection does not require charcoal to carry an independent symbolic power. It links two narrative moments: Peter formerly denies Jesus three times before hostile people; now he can affirm his love three times before fellow disciples. Jesus' provision of breakfast precedes the renewed shepherding commission.

Manning also connects the abundant catch with the original calling known from Luke 5:1–11: the fisherman is summoned again to service. This interconnection is an interpretive proposal; John does not explicitly say that Peter has permanently abandoned discipleship. What the narrative does show is a meeting that leads from past failure into renewed responsibility.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Restoring a Fisherman (John 21:15-17) · 2008-10-02
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2008/10/restoring-fisherman.html

passages.expected_base: The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
passages.rationale:
The thief is identified through leaders who harm the flock
Manning places the saying within Jesus' confrontation with those who expelled the healed man, rather than automatically identifying the thief with Satan.

John 9 ends with leaders insulting and expelling the man Jesus gave sight. The shepherd discourse continues that controversy, contrasting Jesus' care with leadership that steals, kills and scatters. «Thieves» already appear in 10:8 before their conduct is described in verse 10; no change of referent is announced.

Manning adds the background of Ezekiel 34. God condemns Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves, neglecting the sheep and scattering them, then promises to gather the flock and establish his Davidic shepherd. This comparison explains John's contrast without first equating the thief with Satan. Other Jewish texts also apply theft imagery to abusive leaders.

Abundant life stands against that damage and is connected with the good shepherd's care. The application includes discerning authorities who exploit people. Identifying the thief with these leaders does not deny other biblical teaching about evil; it specifies who is being confronted in this discourse.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Misinterpreting the Thief (John 10:10) · 2016-04-28
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2016/misinterpreting-the-thief-john-10-10
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/03/good-shepherd-john-10.html

passages.expected_base: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
passages.rationale:
The good shepherd fulfills Ezekiel's promise
Jesus' self-giving contrasts with shepherds who exploit the sheep and abandon them.

Calling himself the good shepherd is more than choosing a comforting rural image. Ezekiel 34 accuses Israel's leaders of pursuing their own benefit while the flock becomes scattered. God promises to seek the sheep himself and provide a shepherd called David. Manning reads Jesus' discourse against that background.

John has just described religious leaders expelling the healed man (9:34), while Jesus seeks and receives him (9:35). The contrast develops through the hired hand who flees danger and the shepherd who gives his life for the sheep (10:11–13). Jesus' authority is defined by action on their behalf.

For Manning, the imagery brings together promised divine care and the expected Davidic king. Giving his life anticipates the cross. The scene therefore also supplies a criterion for leadership: the flock does not exist to sustain the shepherd; the true shepherd bears the cost of protecting it.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Reading John · 2011-02-15
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/03/good-shepherd-john-10.html

passages.expected_base: For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin.
passages.rationale:
A believer's slavery or helplessness before Christ?
Manning reads the «I» as someone attempting to obey the law without the liberation described in Romans 8.

The present-tense «I am carnal, sold under sin» sounds autobiographical, and many understand it as Paul's Christian experience. Manning defends another reading: Paul represents a person under the law and explains how sin uses a good commandment to produce death, the question raised in 7:13.

His argument compares descriptions across Romans. This «I» is sold under sin (7:14) and taken captive (7:23), whereas believers have been freed from sin (6:18,22) and its enslaving law (8:2). They are also described as no longer in the flesh but in the Spirit (8:9). Manning finds these contrasts difficult to preserve if both conditions describe the same Christian state.

He acknowledges the difficulty of present-tense first-person language but points to Paul's use of a representative «I». He does not deny Christian struggles with sin: he locates that discussion in 8:10–14, where the Spirit enables resistance. This remains a debated interpretation rather than an answer eliminating every autobiographical objection.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Paul is not Talking about Himself: Why I take the "pre-Christian" Reading of Romans 7:14-25 · 2012-04-27
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2012/paul-is-not-talking-about-himself-why-i-take-the-pre-christian-reading-of-romans-7-14-25
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/10/today-in-my-undergraduate-class-on.html
passages.editorial_audit: Manning favors a rhetorical pre-Christian speaker; a Christian autobiographical reading also exists. Retain first person and present tense rather than rewriting the grammar to settle the debate.

passages.expected_base: Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.
passages.rationale:
Punctuation and the statement about Christ
Manning reads «God over all» as continuing the description of Christ, rather than beginning a separate blessing of the Father.

The verse can be punctuated as «Christ…, who is God over all» or as «Christ… . God, who is over all, be blessed». The difference involves sentence boundaries and the referent of the following phrase, rather than a different set of Greek words. Ancient punctuation does not settle it as a modern edition might.

Manning favors connecting the description with Christ. He emphasizes ho ōn, «the one who is», which normally resumes an earlier referent: here, Christ. Taking it to introduce the following noun «God» as a new recipient of praise is less natural in his judgment.

Context matters too: Paul lists Israel's privileges while grieving rejection of Christ. The statement would culminate by identifying the greatness of the one descended from Israel according to the flesh. The separate-doxology reading has defenders and arguments from Paul's other usage; Manning gives greater weight to this sentence's grammar and sequence than to requiring an identical formula elsewhere.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · "Christ who is over all God blessed forever" (Romans 9:5) · 2010-05-31
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2010/05/christ-who-is-over-all-god-blessed.html
passages.editorial_audit: Manning connects God over all with Christ. A doxology addressed to the Father depends on different punctuation. KJV already reflects the first reading; retain it while acknowledging the alternative.

passages.expected_base: Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come.
passages.rationale:
«Not» and «not yet»: two readings and a question of timing
Jesus' later journey requires attention to the manuscript variant and the public appearance his brothers propose.

Jesus' brothers want him to display himself publicly at the feast. He says his time has not come, then travels secretly (7:10). Some manuscripts read «I am not going»; others read «not yet», as the KJV does. This variation explains differences among translations.

Manning also proposes a possible double meaning: going «up» and the outstanding time could anticipate Jesus' glorification through death, resurrection and ascension. He nevertheless acknowledges the simpler explanation: «going up» is ordinary language for traveling to Jerusalem. Jesus can reject the proposed public display without ruling out a later, private journey.

Manning's original manuscript list reverses the evidence: P66, P75 and B support «not yet», while Sinaiticus is among witnesses for «not», as the NET textual note records. Correcting that error prevents its use as evidence. The possible glorification allusion remains a proposal and should not be inserted into Jesus' words.

passages.expected_base: And every man went unto his own house.
passages.rationale:
Where a transmission difficulty begins
The woman-accused-of-adultery story occupies different manuscript positions; this verse begins that unit.

The return of everyone to their homes opens John 7:53–8:11. Although integrated into the KJV and RV1909, this unit is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John preserving this section. Later copies place it elsewhere in John and even in Luke. These differences distinguish the story's transmission from the Gospel's continuous text.

Manning also observes vocabulary and style unlike John's usual writing. He concludes that the unit did not belong to John's original composition, while considering it a potentially authentic early tradition about Jesus. His assessment of its historicity is not something manuscript placement alone proves.

The issue therefore concerns the textual provenance of the complete scene, rather than a moral defect in its content or grounds for silently deleting this verse. This edition retains its base text and makes the difficulty visible so that readers understand what is being compared.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Adulterous Woman (John 8) · 2009-06-29
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/06/adulterous-woman.html

passages.expected_base: Jesus went unto the mount of Olives.
passages.rationale:
A familiar scene with a disputed textual frame
Jesus' journey to the Mount of Olives belongs to the same variably transmitted unit as his encounter with the woman.

This verse can look like an unquestionable transition between two days. It nevertheless belongs to John 7:53–8:11: the temple scene, adultery accusation and Jesus' response circulate as one unit. When an edition notes that the episode is absent from early witnesses, that observation includes this introductory sentence.

Manning combines its absence from early manuscripts of John with its displacement to other locations in later copies. He also notes differences in style and vocabulary. His conclusion is that a tradition about Jesus entered the Gospel during transmission, distinguishing the story's possible antiquity from Johannine authorship.

The Mount of Olives situates the received narrative but does not establish its origin by itself. Retaining the verse while explaining its textual frame allows the story to be read without treating a question requiring comparison of manuscripts, locations and the whole unit's language as already settled.

passages.expected_base: She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.
passages.rationale:
Mercy together with the call to leave sin
The ending joins rejection of hypocritical condemnation with a demand for change; it does not make adultery morally indifferent.

After the accusers withdraw, Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned the woman. Her answer leads to two closing statements: he does not condemn her, and she must sin no more. Manning emphasizes their combination. Compassion for the accused neither removes sin's seriousness nor endorses manipulation of the law against her.

The preceding scene tests Jesus through an adultery case. His reference to casting the first stone recalls witnesses' responsibility in Deuteronomy 17:7 and directs attention back to the accusers. Identifying their exact guilt is harder than recognizing the exposure of hypocrisy.

The whole episode, including this ending, has a disputed textual history (7:53–8:11). Manning regards it as a true tradition about Jesus subsequently inserted into John; that is his historical assessment, rather than a certainty imposed by this note. The edition preserves its received words while explaining both the narrative and its textual situation.

passages.expected_base: And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
passages.text: And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.
passages.rationale:
Darkness that neither understands nor overcomes the light
Manning proposes that the opening verb anticipates two responses to Jesus developed throughout the Gospel.

Katalambanō can describe understanding something or overtaking and overcoming it. Hence translations vary between darkness failing to comprehend the light and failing to overcome it. Choosing one expression can omit a resonance Manning regards as deliberate.

The prologue introduces themes subsequently acted out. Nicodemus misunderstands birth from above, while others take Jesus' language about water and bread materially. His opponents also attempt to seize and kill him, yet opposition does not have the final word over the light. The narrative develops both possibilities associated with the verb.

Manning additionally connects «comprehended not», «received him not» and those who «received him» (1:5,11–12), using related Greek verbs. The proposed double meaning arises from this narrative pattern; it does not mean every occurrence of katalambanō always contains both senses. The note makes visible what a single English rendering can struggle to convey.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Prolog of John (John 1:1-18) · 2009-01-28
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/01/prolog-of-john.html
passages.editorial_audit: Katalambano allows comprehend or overcome. Record the possible double resonance as an unapplied proposal rather than silently replacing KJV's reading.

passages.expected_base: Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
passages.text: Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”
passages.rationale:
«Again» and «from above»: Nicodemus' misunderstanding
The need for another birth is explained through its origin in God, rather than physically repeating the first.

Anōthen can mean «again» or «from above». Nicodemus understands the first possibility bodily, asking how someone could enter the womb a second time (3:4). Jesus' response concerns the Spirit and life whose origin cannot be reduced to human ancestry.

Manning regards the double meaning as organizing the dialogue. Israel's teacher acknowledges that Jesus comes from God but still interprets his teaching within ordinary birth. «From above» connects the statement with Jesus' heavenly origin and the birth from God announced in the prologue (1:12–13).

Nicodemus' confusion helps readers move from an insufficient understanding to Jesus' explanation. «Born again» is therefore not an absurd translation: it preserves the sense that makes the character's question possible. The note restores the dimension that wording may obscure: new life comes from God and the Spirit, rather than from repeating a biological process.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jesus and Nicodemus (John 3) · 2009-02-23
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/02/jesus-and-nicodemus.html

passages.expected_base: The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
passages.rationale:
Wind illuminates the Spirit and the new birth
The comparison describes recognizable action whose origin and destination do not come under human control.

Pneuma can mean either wind or Spirit. The sentence speaks of blowing and sound but concludes with the person born of the Spirit. Moving between these senses allows an everyday experience—hearing wind without mastering its course—to illuminate the birth Jesus describes.

Manning connects this with Nicodemus' misunderstanding. Such life originates «from above» and cannot be understood solely through ordinary birth. He also sees a relationship with Jesus: throughout John, people fail to recognize where he comes from and where he is going.

The saying does not make believers directionless or morally unaccountable. Its comparison concerns the origin and destiny of life produced by the Spirit, rather than declaring every impulse divine guidance. Recognizing the wordplay preserves the image without reducing it to meteorology or turning it into permission for arbitrary behavior.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jesus and Nicodemus (John 3) · 2009-02-23

passages.expected_base: And Jesus said unto him, Friend, wherefore art thou come? Then came they, and laid hands on Jesus, and took him.
passages.text: Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you have come to do.” Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him.
passages.rationale:
Does Jesus question Judas or tell him to act?
The Greek is elliptical; Manning prefers an implied command while acknowledging that the question remains possible.

«Friend, wherefore art thou come?» and «Friend, do what you have come for» sound different. Both resolve the brief expression eph' ho parei, approximately «for what you are here». No explicit «do» appears, and modern punctuation cannot simply be assumed in ancient witnesses.

Manning favors supplying a command. He notes the scarcity of comparable questions with that opening in the New Testament and Greek Old Testament, and compares the unambiguous instruction to Judas in John 13:27 to act quickly. That narrative parallel helps without independently proving Matthew's syntax.

«Friend» does not make the betrayal innocent: the same address confronts someone in Matthew 20:13 and 22:12. The kiss still identifies Jesus to those coming to arrest him. The alternative remains an explained proposal rather than a claim that the Greek words remove all ambiguity.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Judas' Kiss (Matthew 26:50, John 13:27) · 2009-05-13

passages.expected_base: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
passages.rationale:
Going out to welcome the arriving Lord
Manning compares the meeting with a public reception for a ruler, within Paul's comfort concerning believers who have died.

The concern of 4:13–18 is whether the dead in Christ will miss his coming. Paul answers that they will rise and join living believers with the Lord. «Caught up» describes being taken or snatched away; the following phrase gives its purpose: meeting him.

Manning examines apantēsis and related words used when people go outside a city to welcome a dignitary and accompany the arrival. He compares the welcome to Jesus in John 12:13 and Roman Christians going out to meet Paul in Acts 28:15. He reads this as the descending Lord's triumphal reception, shared by living and resurrected believers.

That background supports his interpretation of welcome rather than an emphasis on escaping earth. The word alone supplies neither a complete end-times timetable nor a resolution of every question about subsequent destination. The passage's consolation rests on reunion with Christ and the participation of all who belong to him.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Snatched Up For a Meeting · 2014-10-16
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2014/snatched-up-for-a-meeting

passages.expected_base: And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King!
passages.rationale:
«Preparation of the Passover»: a chronological proposal
Manning understands the phrase as Friday of Passover week, without treating this harmonization as undisputed.

The wording can appear to place Jesus' condemnation before the Passover meal, whereas the Synoptic Gospels describe the last supper as Passover. John 18:28 adds the leaders' wish to remain undefiled so they can eat it. These references must be explained rather than ignored when aligning the accounts.

Manning notes that paraskeuē, «preparation», became a designation for Friday, when households prepared for the Sabbath. John 19:31 connects this preparation with the following Sabbath, and Mark 15:42 explains it explicitly. He proposes «Friday of Passover week» and understands eating Passover as potentially including other festival meals, rather than only its opening supper.

He accordingly considers it possible that John and the Synoptics refer to the same day. The solution depends on the expressions' scope and competes with other chronological explanations. This note preserves that status, presenting Manning's reasons without turning a reconstruction of dates into an added certainty in the verse.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Chronology of Easter in John and the Synoptic Gospels · 2015-03-30
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2015/chronology-of-easter-in-john-and-the-synoptic-gospels

passages.expected_base: For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
passages.rationale:
Three days: a Jonah comparison, not a stopwatch
Manning explains the expression through inclusive reckoning and the rescue theme connecting Jonah's sign with resurrection.

If «three days and three nights» must mean exactly 72 hours, death on Friday and an empty tomb on Sunday appear incompatible. Manning observes that the accounts alternate «after three days», «in three days» and «on the third day». Esther 4:16–5:1 provides a parallel: a fast described as three days, night and day, leads to action «on the third day».

Counting is not the whole emphasis. Jonah describes his descent as approaching death and his rescue as life restored (Jonah 2:2,6). Jesus compares this experience with his own death and emergence from the grave. The analogy does not identify him with Jonah's disobedience; it selects the pattern of descent and deliverance.

Manning also connects the third day in Luke 18:33 with restoration in Hosea 6:1–2, treating it as a proposed allusion. Matthew's explicit comparison remains Jonah's sign: the decisive outcome is Jesus' vindication after death.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Three Days and Three Nights · 2015-04-01
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2015/three-days-and-three-nights

passages.expected_base: And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
passages.rationale:
Temple stones and a restoration reversed
Manning hears an echo of Haggai: what was rebuilt can again come under judgment.

The disciples admire the temple buildings and Jesus announces their demolition. Manning connects «stone upon stone» with the Greek wording of Haggai 2:15, where the prophet recalls the period before the sanctuary's rebuilding. A comparatively unusual phrase used for the same subject makes an allusion plausible.

The contrast would be deliberate. In Haggai, renewed building accompanies a call to return to God and a promise of blessing; Matthew's warning announces the desolation of what had symbolized restoration. The building's magnificence cannot itself guarantee a faithful response to God.

Manning also addresses a visual objection. The surviving Western Wall belonged to the platform's retaining structure, rather than to the temple buildings the disciples pointed out. Its survival therefore does not itself contradict the prediction. The proposed Haggai connection supplies a theological reading without making verbal similarity an automatic proof of intention.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · No Stone Left Unturned: Solving a Minor Mystery · 2013-05-21
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2013/no-stone-left-unturned-solving-a-minor-mystery

passages.expected_base: And now, I pray you, consider from this day and upward, from before a stone was laid upon a stone in the temple of the Lord:
passages.rationale:
Remembering the temple before its rebuilding
«Stone upon stone» leads Manning to compare Haggai's restoration with Jesus' later announcement of destruction.

Haggai asks the people to consider their circumstances before renewed work on the temple. The inadequate harvests of the following verses belong to that examination: hardship had not brought the expected return to God (2:16–17). Remembering prepares the promise of blessing associated with the new stage (2:19).

Manning highlights the Greek phrase «stone upon stone», which reappears in Jesus' warning concerning the sanctuary (Matthew 24:2). In Haggai it concerns construction; in the Gospels the structure will be dismantled. Shared wording and subject suggest to him an intentional reversal of restoration.

The parallel situates both passages within faithfulness and judgment instead of treating temple stones as a permanent religious guarantee. The allusion remains Manning's proposal. Haggai directly addresses people called to rebuild and return to God; every detail of their agricultural crisis need not become a prediction of first-century events.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · No Stone Left Unturned: Solving a Minor Mystery · 2013-05-21

passages.expected_base: And let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour; and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith the Lord.
passages.rationale:
A Greek fragment and two ways of saying «each person»
A small translation difference helps identify the passage without announcing a new biblical teaching.

Examining a photograph of fragments announced in 2021, Manning identifies sequences corresponding to «his neighbor» and «in the hearts». Together they suggest Zechariah 8:17, forbidding plans to harm another person. He also reads anēr, «man», where the usual Greek edition has hekastos, «each».

The Hebrew word ish can be translated with either expression in a distributive construction such as «each person… his neighbor». This variant does not turn the prohibition into a different command. It shows an ancient witness preserving another Greek choice for the same general meaning.

Manning's identification is preliminary, based on visible letters rather than a complete reconstruction of the scroll. Fragmentary preservation and the need for better photographs limit conclusions. The contribution illustrates manuscript comparison: readable words, context and translation possibilities work together without presenting missing portions as certain text.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · New Dead Sea Scroll Discovery: A Closer Look · 2021-03-17
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2021/new-dead-sea-scroll-discovery-a-closer-look

passages.expected_base: Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alpheus, and Simon called Zelotes,
passages.rationale:
«Zealot» does not establish that Simon was a guerrilla
Manning distinguishes a zealous person's nickname from a faction name documented decades later.

Simon is often imagined as a former revolutionary who laid down his weapons to follow Jesus. That biography is usually inferred from his epithet alone. Manning observes that zēlōtēs describes someone enthusiastic or zealous for a cause; the word itself implies neither violence nor party membership.

Acts 21:20 describes believers as zealous for the law, and 1 Peter 3:13 speaks of zeal for good. Josephus, by contrast, uses «Zealots» for a particular faction appearing during the Jewish War around AD 67. Applying that organizational name to the Simon of Jesus' ministry requires historical identification that the nickname does not establish.

Manning considers zeal for God or for good the more likely explanation. He acknowledges scholarly disagreement, and Luke does not say when Simon acquired the name. An attractive reconstruction for drama or preaching should therefore not become biographical information supposedly supplied by the verse.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Simon the Zealot was not a Zealot! · 2025-10-08
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2025/simon-the-zealot-was-not-a-zealot
passages.editorial_audit: Zealot may express personal zeal, not necessarily membership in the party of AD 67–70. The correct Mark parallel is 3:18, not 3:8 as printed in the blog.

passages.expected_base: But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
passages.rationale:
Grammatical gender and the Spirit's identity
Greek pronouns agree with nouns; the Spirit's personhood is expressed through his actions rather than an isolated ending.

It is sometimes argued that a masculine pronoun proves the Spirit is a person, whereas a neuter one would suggest an impersonal force. Manning explains that Greek gender does not work that way. Pneuma, «spirit», is neuter; paraklētos, «Helper» or «Comforter», is masculine. Pronouns follow those grammatical relationships.

This verse contains both: the relative pronoun associated with «Holy Spirit» is neuter, while the pronoun referring to the Comforter is masculine. The referent does not change from a thing to a person. Likewise, the neuter noun paidion can designate a human child.

The personal description is conveyed by action: the Spirit teaches, reminds and is sent by the Father. Other passages describe his guidance, speech and grief. English should communicate those relationships naturally without treating the gender of a Greek pronoun as an independent theological demonstration.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Holy Spirit and Grammatical Gender · 2026-02-09
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2026/the-holy-spirit-and-grammatical-gender

passages.expected_base: The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
passages.rationale:
Thomas asks for nail marks, not merely hands
Manning responds to the proposal that nails entered the crucifixion tradition only at a later date.

Thomas demands to see the nail marks and touch the wounds. Jesus subsequently offers his hands and side (20:27). Manning emphasizes this explicit reference against claims that Scripture never says Jesus was nailed or that nailing was undocumented before the Jewish War beginning in AD 66.

His historical argument goes beyond Josephus. Philo, Jesus' contemporary, uses images of people crucified and nailed to wood; Diodorus also describes an execution involving nails before the first century. Such evidence establishes knowledge of the practice before its proposed starting date, without measuring its frequency in every crucifixion.

In John, the wounds identify the risen Jesus with the one who was crucified. The blessing for those who believe without seeing (20:29) does not make the encounter irrelevant: it addresses readers who cannot share Thomas' visual experience. Subsequent faith receives testimony to this meeting rather than a denial of its content.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Yes, Jesus was Crucified with Nails · 2025-04-25
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2025/yes-jesus-was-crucified-with-nails

passages.expected_base: Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.
passages.rationale:
«Born king»: the threat Herod hears
The magi's announcement challenges a ruler whose title depended on Rome and conquest.

Herod already holds the title «King of the Jews». Asking about someone born with that title is therefore no harmless religious compliment. Drawing on Josephus, Manning explains the contrast: Herod did not descend from the ruling dynasty, had Idumean origins and received Roman senatorial recognition before taking Jerusalem by force.

Marriage into the Hasmonean family strengthened his connection with the former royal house but did not remove his fear of rivals. Executions within his own family show how far he could go to defend power. The announcement of a newborn king accordingly explains alarm leading to violence.

The title returns at the end of Jesus' life, in interrogation, soldiers' mockery and the cross inscription. Manning contrasts kingship secured through appointment and conquest with the kingship Matthew announces at birth and displays again in the passion. The background illuminates Herod's reaction without inventing a conversation the Gospel does not report.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Herod, the King of the Jews · 2024-12-23
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2024/herod-the-king-of-the-jews
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/12/herod-remembered.html

passages.expected_base: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
passages.rationale:
Receiving Jesus and believing describe the same children of God
The sentence structure does not divide them into two groups or make receiving a separate act detached from faith.

After «his own received him not», John describes those who do receive him and identifies them as those believing in his name. Manning observes that these expressions concern the same people, to whom Jesus grants authority to become God's children. They are not disconnected stages or privileges assigned to different groups.

Verse 13 continues with another description of them: they have been born of God. Tracing the clauses makes it possible to read the whole sentence without losing its relationships among receiving, believing and divine birth.

The opening disciples illustrate welcoming Jesus through listening, recognition and following. Biological ancestry or membership in a people does not itself confer the identity described in the prologue. Manning emphasizes the Father's action as the origin of this family, while the Gospel develops the content of believing who Jesus is and what he does.

passages.expected_base: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
passages.rationale:
Children through birth from God, not human ancestry
Three negatives prepare the central affirmation about the origin of those who receive Jesus.

«Not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man» accumulates descriptions of human birth. Manning does not assign three independent salvation theories to these phrases. Together they deny that natural origin is sufficient to make someone God's child.

The sentence continues describing those who receive Jesus and believe in his name (1:12). These people are the subject of «which were born… of God». In Greek, the birth verb stands near «from God» at the sentence's end, strengthening the contrast after the negatives. English word order can make that emphasis less apparent.

John soon develops the encounter with Nicodemus, Israel's teacher who must understand birth from above. Neither family membership nor religious credentials can produce the divine birth that gives this life. Manning's contribution clarifies the clauses' relationships and the children's identity without reducing the verse to a discussion of reproduction.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · "Children of God" (John 1:13) · 2012-10-15

passages.expected_base: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
passages.rationale:
Grace as the generosity that gives salvation
Manning reconnects «grace» with favor and gift, rather than an earned reward.

A familiar church word can become a technical label repeated without understanding. Manning suggests hearing charis here as generosity or a generous gift: salvation originates with God rather than constituting wages owed to people who accumulate merit. Verses 8–9 explicitly contrast works and the grounds for boasting.

Romans 4:4 provides a useful comparison. Wages due to a worker are reckoned as obligation, not favor. That contrast illuminates the character of the gift in Ephesians. Faith is the means of reception without turning God's giving into a commercial obligation.

Manning also distinguishes grace from mercy without rigidly separating them: mercy addresses need, while grace emphasizes the giver's generosity. He does not propose replacing charis mechanically with one word throughout the New Testament. Context governs its nuance; here the point is recognizing God as saving through giving rather than paying a debt owed to the recipient.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Generous Charis · 2011-05-02
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2011/generous-charis
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/06/grace-and-mercy.html

passages.expected_base: Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
passages.rationale:
Wages explain what a gift is not
The contrast between obligation and grace clarifies why justification is not presented as a debt God must pay.

Someone who completes agreed work is entitled to wages. Paying them does not require special generosity from the employer; an obligation exists. Paul uses that ordinary experience after citing Abraham's faith and before describing trust in God who justifies the ungodly (4:3–5).

Manning emphasizes charis as favor or generosity. The payment is «not reckoned of grace» because it is not entered as a freely given present, but as something due. The sentence makes grace intelligible within ordinary language about giving and receiving rather than requiring a detached religious definition.

The analogy does not disparage honest work or declare human effort worthless in every setting. Its function is to identify the basis of the relationship under discussion: claiming payment contrasts with trusting the God who gives. This also illuminates salvation by grace in Ephesians 2:8–9 and prevents treating merit as making salvation an enforceable wage.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Generous Charis · 2011-05-02
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2011/generous-charis

passages.expected_base: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
passages.rationale:
What a papyrus can contribute to a disputed word
Manning examines a business dispute to clarify authentein; the document does not itself settle the church instruction's scope.

The verb authenteō occurs in BGU 1208, an Egyptian business letter predating the New Testament. It has been cited in debates over whether 1 Timothy prohibits exercising authority or assuming it abusively. Manning reconstructs the broader letter because quoting a phrase without identifying its participants can distort the comparison.

Tryphon reports transport and pricing difficulties to Asclepiades. Manning understands earlier legal action as giving him leverage over Antilochos, so he renders the verbal form as exercising or asserting authority. He questions reconstructions making Tryphon a tax official or the other party a slave, identities the document does not establish.

The papyrus has gaps, difficult commercial language and partly reconstructed relationships. A word describing authority in this negotiation does not automatically determine whether authority elsewhere is legitimate, usurped or abusive. This is a limited lexical control, to be combined with 1 Timothy's syntax and argument rather than made to settle the entire ecclesial debate.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · BGU 1208: Translation and Explanation
https://biblethinker.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/FINAL-BGU-1208-Translation-and-Notes.pdf

passages.expected_base: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
passages.rationale:
Why et is not a hidden name of Jesus
Connecting aleph-tav with «Alpha and Omega» focuses on a particle's letters while overlooking its role in the sentence.

Manning responds to questions about a video claiming to find Jesus inside the Hebrew of Genesis 1:1. Its reasoning joins three ideas: Jesus is the Logos, he is called «Alpha and Omega», and the first and last Hebrew letters are aleph and tav. Because those letters form et, the particle is treated as his hidden name in creation.

The supposed reference stands between «God» and «the heavens». There et marks the heavens as the direct object of «created»; it occurs again, with «and», before the earth. English expresses that relationship through sentence construction without a separate equivalent word. A personal name has not thereby been omitted.

Manning tests the proposal against other occurrences: the same particle introduces the ground watered in Genesis 2:6 and Nimrod in 10:8. Turning it consistently into Jesus' name would generate thousands of nonsensical readings. Linking the endpoints of two alphabets does not alter its grammatical function. Christ's relationship to creation must be argued from texts expressing it, rather than attributed to these two letters.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jesus the Aleph-Tav? (Genesis 1:1, Revelation 21:6) · 2009-10-31
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/10/few-people-asked-me-about-nature-of.html

comment_review_history.note_title: A hidden name for Jesus in Genesis 1:1?
comment_review_history.note_lead: A claim circulated in videos and blogs identifies the Hebrew particle אֵת with Jesus.
comment_review_history.note_body:
Readers asked Manning about a video promoting this claim. The proposed link runs from Alpha and Omega, the ends of the Greek alphabet, to aleph and tav, the ends of the Hebrew alphabet. Those letters spell אֵת (et), found between God and the heavens in the Hebrew sentence.

But אֵת marks what God created: it introduces the heavens and appears again before the earth. English expresses the relationship without a separate equivalent. No name for Jesus has therefore been omitted. Substituting Jesus for the particle would place him among what was created, changing the sentence. Christ’s role in creation must be established from passages teaching it, rather than this substitution.

A claim circulated in videos and blogs identifies the Hebrew particle אֵת with Jesus.

passages.expected_base: Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.
passages.rationale:
Why 666 is not a hidden Arabic phrase
Manning answers an identification with Islam based on rotating letters in a late manuscript.

The claim he challenges says that turning the 666 signs reveals weapons and the Arabic expression bismillah. Manning first observes that John asks readers to calculate a number, rather than rotate a picture. Greek numerical notation uses chi, xi and stigma for 600, 60 and 6; a mark above them indicates numerical use.

He also checks the witness described as fourth-century Vaticanus. The Revelation text used in the comparison belongs to a fifteenth-century supplement, not the ancient portion of the codex. Early copies write the number differently, sometimes in full words. The alleged Arabic picture depends on one much later handwriting style.

Manning favors relating the name's numerical value to Nero. That identification remains open to discussion, but rejecting it does not validate the graphic theory. Its decisive weakness is confusing numerical writing with an inscription whose appearance requires arbitrary rotations and rearrangements.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Mark of the Beast is Islam? Walid Shoebat and 666 · 2010-07-13

passages.expected_base: Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled.
passages.rationale:
«This generation» and the temple's destruction
Manning retains the ordinary meaning of generation and distinguishes Jerusalem's signs from the unknown time of Christ's return.

To address an apparently unfulfilled prediction, some render genea as «race» or «people of promise». Manning observes that this is not the best explanation of its other New Testament uses. He starts instead with Jesus' contemporary generation and the temple question that prompts the discourse (24:2–3).

He relates the conflicts, false messiahs, persecution and desolation of 24:5–25 to the crisis culminating in AD 70. He reads «these things» within that setting and distinguishes the Son of Man's coming, whose day remains unknown (24:36). The verse therefore does not supply him with a date for the final return.

Manning acknowledges that his solution leaves difficulties, particularly the continuity and proximity language of 24:29–34. Those tensions should remain visible. His practical conclusion follows the subsequent parables: disciples remain faithful to their task rather than redefining a word to secure a timetable.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · This Generation Will Not Pass Away (Matthew 24:34) · 2009-05-07

passages.expected_base: If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.
passages.rationale:
Costly loyalty chosen with open eyes
Manning reads «hate» alongside Matthew's family conflict and the parables requiring calculation of discipleship's cost.

The wording can sound like a command to feel hostility toward family or give a leader blind devotion. Manning attends to what follows: before constructing a tower or entering a war, people calculate whether they can bear the cost (14:28–32). Following Jesus requires conscious decision rather than abandoning judgment.

Matthew 10:37–38 expresses the parallel as loving parents or children «more than» Jesus, within a warning about household division. Manning understands both passages as loyalty that may require a choice when family demands abandoning Jesus. The reference to one's own life extends this to the possibility of death.

The point is not manufacturing conflicts or neglecting family duties to display zeal. The demand becomes concrete when loyalties cannot both be maintained. The parables prevent minimizing the cost while also preventing faith from becoming unthinking allegiance: disciples must recognize the choice and what it may require.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Blind Devotion? (Luke 14:26) · 2008-04-25
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2008/04/blind-devotion.html

passages.expected_base: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.
passages.rationale:
The tree's birds and a kingdom offering shelter
Manning connects the mustard seed with Ezekiel 17 instead of automatically importing the birds' meaning from another parable.

In the sower parable, birds represent the evil one snatching away seed (13:19). It does not follow that birds must mean the same thing in every parable. Here they nest in a plant that has grown remarkably; their function within the picture differs.

Manning compares sheltering royal trees in Ezekiel 17:23, 31:6 and Daniel 4:12. He favors Ezekiel 17, where God plants a small shoot that becomes a cedar sheltering birds of every kind. Its royal-restoration setting illuminates the contrast between modest beginnings and greatness offering refuge.

The small band surrounding Jesus therefore does not measure the kingdom's value or eventual reach. The proposed allusion is more than a botanical observation and does not turn every bird into a corrupting agent. Interpretation depends on the whole scene and its kingdom background rather than assigning a fixed meaning to a symbol wherever it occurs.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Kingdom for the Birds? (Matthew 13:31-32) · 2008-04-04

passages.expected_base: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
passages.rationale:
The king at God's right hand and its application to Christ
Manning begins with the psalm's royal language to explain its New Testament use for Jesus.

The opening presents God addressing the psalmist's lord and granting him honor while his enemies are subdued. Manning reads the whole as a blessing over Israel's king: rule amid enemies, willing participation and victory give the poem its setting. That framework prevents detaching the sentence from the royal scene it develops.

The New Testament returns to it in Matthew 22:41–46, Acts 2:34–36 and Hebrews 1:13, applying it to the Messiah, David's son exalted by God. For Manning, this brings the psalm to a christological culmination rather than requiring denial that its language could address a historical Israelite king.

The priestly title involving Melchizedek belongs to the same royal portrait (110:4) and receives fuller treatment in Hebrews. Reconstructions about inherited titles in ancient Jerusalem remain historical hypotheses, not facts demonstrated by verse 1. Keeping that distinction preserves the royal argument without making the hypotheses textual certainties.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · That Melchizedek Guy (Psalm 110, Hebrews 5-7) · 2008-06-23
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2008/06/question-what-is-culturalhistorical.html

passages.expected_base: Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.
passages.rationale:
Blessedness opens a whole poem delighting in instruction
The psalm's alphabetic structure invites each stanza to be read within its sustained celebration of God's word.

The opening beatitude does not introduce an isolated checklist. The psalm has 22 eight-verse stanzas corresponding to Hebrew alphabet letters; within each stanza, every line begins with the same letter. This crafted structure sustains an extensive exploration of God's instruction.

Manning illustrates the point particularly through 119:9–16. Its first line asks about keeping one's way pure, but the rest develops seeking, keeping, treasuring, learning, speaking and delighting in the word. Imposing the modern expectation that an opening sentence summarizes an entire paragraph reduces the stanza to a purity technique and misses its poetic celebration.

Applied to the psalm's beginning, blessed walking in the law opens into this fuller relationship with God. Obedience matters, encompassing thought, affection and action. The poem seeks more than a completed reading quota: it expresses a life learning to delight in received instruction.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Torah, Torah, Rah Rah Rah! (Psalm 119) · 2008-06-17
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2008/06/torah-torah-rah-rah-rah.html

Applied to the psalm's beginning, blessed walking in the law opens into this fuller relationship with God. Obedience matters, encompassing thought, affection and action. The poem seeks more than a completed reading quota: it expresses a life learning to delight in received instruction.

passages.expected_base: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison;
passages.rationale:
The «spirits in prison» and the limits of reconstruction
Manning questions whether one difficult sentence can establish a detailed account of Jesus' activity between death and resurrection.

The expression is used to argue that Jesus descended into hell, preached to the damned or released ancient faithful people. Manning distinguishes the text from these fuller reconstructions. It mentions proclamation to spirits connected with disobedience in Noah's time, without explaining everything those accounts add.

He acknowledges several possibilities: human spirits or spiritual powers; a proclamation of victory; or Christ's Spirit speaking through Noah, in connection with 1 Peter 1:10–11. «In prison» may describe their situation at the time of writing without necessarily locating them there when the proclamation occurred. The sequence and timing remain disputed.

His objection concerns building a detailed itinerary on one reading of an especially difficult passage, rather than doubting Christ's victory. The note preserves alternatives and the context of victory and suffering. The Gospels' silence about those intervening days does not become a conclusive demonstration of any one reconstruction.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Harrowing of Hell? · 2008-06-13
