passages.expected_base: Judge not, that ye be not judged.
passages.rationale:
One's own beam changes how another is corrected
Manning reads the prohibition within a paragraph condemning hypocritical judgment and preparing responsible help.

«Judge not» is often treated as prohibiting every moral evaluation. The paragraph, however, continues: first remove the beam from your own eye, then help with the speck in your brother's (7:3–5). The problem is presuming to correct someone else's fault while tolerating a greater fault in oneself.

Manning compares Galatians 6:1–5, where restoring someone requires humility and attention to one's own conduct. Correction aims to help rather than display superiority or humiliate. Discerning harmful conduct and condemning someone proudly are not identical activities.

The warning retains its force because it addresses the corrector too. The image does not permit ignoring verse 1 after a superficial self-check; it calls for a different disposition toward the person being served. The whole paragraph supports recognizing wrong and seeking restoration without turning judgment into permission for harshness or a ban on all mutual responsibility.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Judge Not? (Matthew 7:1-6) · 2009-01-19
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/01/judge-not.html

passages.expected_base: Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.
passages.rationale:
The Lord's will takes shape in the new life
Manning explains it through Ephesians' ethical contrasts rather than a secret key to choosing a job or spouse.

«Understanding what the will of the Lord is» may first suggest discovering which major individual decision to make. The paragraph belongs instead to a sequence beginning in 4:22–24: putting off former conduct and putting on the new self.

Manning follows its concrete oppositions: falsehood and truth, theft and work enabling generosity, harmful speech and words that build up, bitterness and forgiveness. Chapter 5 continues with foolishness and wisdom, drunkenness and being filled with the Spirit. The instruction thus receives accessible content: learning conduct corresponding to the Lord.

Praise, thanksgiving and mutual submission follow in 5:18–21. The phrase does not itself promise to select a career, address or marriage. Nor does it make such choices irrelevant; it clarifies the life that should characterize them. Manning's point is that no private sign is needed before recognizing truthfulness, generosity and forgiveness as part of God's will.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Not this... but that. (Ephesians 4-5) · 2010-10-06
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2010/10/not-this-but-that-ephesians-4-5.html

passages.expected_base: Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?
passages.rationale:
«Come, see»: an invitation prompted by surprising knowledge
Manning proposes an Elisha echo while acknowledging that this parallel is weaker than others in the series.

The woman invites her town to meet someone who knows her personal history. Her question about the Messiah follows her recognition of Jesus as a prophet (4:19). The invitation is grounded in what he has revealed, allowing others to consider his identity.

Manning compares 2 Kings 6:12–13. Elisha knows even the Syrian king's private words, and the king orders a search for him. The Greek version uses wording similar to «come, see». Both narratives direct attention toward a man with extraordinary knowledge, though the intentions differ: capture in Kings, bringing others to Jesus in John.

Shared wording alone cannot prove an allusion; comparable invitations occur elsewhere. Manning considers it possible within John's broader Elijah-Elisha pattern. Its uncertainty should remain visible. The clear narrative point is the woman's testimony and the response leading her community toward Jesus.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I am Not Elijah, Part 1 (John 4:29, 2 Kings 6:12-13) · 2009-11-28
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/11/i-am-not-elijah-part-1-john-429-2-kings.html

passages.expected_base: Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
passages.rationale:
Jesus' reply to Mary and a possible Elisha echo
The idiom «what to me and to you?» marks distance from the request; Manning compares a narrative that also ends in unexpected help.

Read literally, the question sounds puzzling. It is a known biblical Greek idiom for distancing oneself or challenging an intervention. The narrative difficulty remains: Jesus appears to decline Mary's request but subsequently remedies the shortage.

Following Edward Klink's study, Manning compares 2 Kings 3:9–20. Kings lack water; Elisha answers with the same idiom, gives instructions and provision follows. Cana similarly combines shortage, request, an initially distancing response and unusual instructions leading to abundance. The whole pattern gives the parallel more weight than an isolated phrase.

The proposed connection places Jesus alongside the great prophets, while the sign manifests his glory and strengthens the disciples' faith (2:11). It does not make Mary morally equivalent to the king Elisha confronts or transfer every detail between stories. Jesus' «hour» remains a distinctive Johannine element to preserve.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I Am Not Elijah, Part 2 (John 2:3-4, 2 Kings 3:9-22) · 2009-11-27

passages.expected_base: There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink.
passages.rationale:
The one asking for water offers life
Manning compares Jesus and the Samaritan woman with Elijah and the widow of Zarephath: a modest request opens into greater provision.

Jesus arrives tired and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. His need is real, not simply scenery for displaying knowledge. The roles then reverse: the one requesting water offers water leading to eternal life (4:10–14).

Manning relates the sequence to 1 Kings 17:8–16. Elijah asks a foreign widow for water and food; she is herself needy but receives a promise that flour and oil will last through the crisis. Both encounters begin with a request to a woman outside Israel and disclose the generosity of Israel's God.

The wording is not an exact quotation, and the narratives retain differences. Manning finds the connection stronger because John's next sign recalls another Elijah episode involving a son's life (4:46–54). The comparison illuminates Jesus' identity and gift without reducing the woman to a symbol or erasing the concrete assistance he requests.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I Am Not Elijah, Part 3 (John 4:7, 1 Kings 17:10-14) · 2009-11-26

Manning finds the connection stronger because John's next sign recalls another Elijah episode involving a son's life (4:46–54). The comparison illuminates Jesus' identity and gift without reducing the woman to a symbol or erasing the concrete assistance he requests.

passages.expected_base: Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way.
passages.rationale:
«Your son lives»: believing before verification
The repeated saying connects trust in Jesus' word with the theme of life and an Elijah echo.

The father asks Jesus to come before his son dies. Jesus tells him to go and declares the son alive. The man believes before meeting servants who confirm the healing. He then recognizes its timing and believes with his household (4:51–53), showing the development of trust.

Manning highlights the three repetitions of the son's life. He compares 1 Kings 17:23–24, where Elijah returns the living child to the widow, who acknowledges the truth of God's word in his mouth. In both narratives, life restored leads to recognition of God's representative.

The scenes are not identical: Elijah is beside a dead child, while Jesus heals a still-living child at a distance. Their differences should remain visible rather than merging John's official with other Gospel characters. The point extends beyond an extraordinary cure: Jesus gives life, and his word calls for trust before the father can see confirmation.

passages.expected_base: There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
passages.rationale:
Barley loaves connect the sign with Elisha
Scarce food, a servant's objection and leftovers form a concrete narrative comparison.

«What are they among so many?» expresses the disparity between five loaves, two fish and the crowd. John specifies barley loaves. Manning compares 2 Kings 4:42–44, where Elisha orders twenty barley loaves distributed among a hundred people and his servant objects that they cannot suffice.

Both narratives combine a command to feed, the servant's attention to insufficiency, satisfied people and food left over. John describes a much larger crowd and twelve baskets of fragments, magnifying the provision as well as associating Jesus with Elisha. The nearby Passover reference also prepares the bread-of-life discourse.

The argument does not derive meaning from an isolated ingredient. It brings food, participants, objection, command and outcome together. Visible resources do not delimit Jesus' gift; the subsequent conversation asks what life he offers and how people should respond.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I Am Not Elijah, Part 5 (John 6:9-13, 2 Kings 4:42-44) · 2009-11-25

passages.expected_base: And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.
passages.rationale:
«Go, wash»: healing that leads to recognition
The Naaman comparison helps Manning explain the sequence of command, washing, healing and faith.

Jesus places mud on the man's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. He obeys and returns seeing. Manning connects the episode with 2 Kings 5, where Elisha directs Naaman to wash in the Jordan and healing leads to acknowledgment of Israel's God.

The commands are similar in meaning but do not use identical Greek verbs: washing part of the body differs linguistically from bathing the whole person. That difference prevents treating the parallel as a literal quotation. Its support lies in the action sequence and outcomes, alongside other Elisha echoes Manning identifies in John.

The healed man subsequently advances in his confession of Jesus as prophet, one from God and Lord. Translating Siloam as «Sent» fits this concern with identity, though the detail's exact function is debatable. The sign's force does not lie in autonomous power of water or mud, but in who gives sight and the response to receiving it.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I Am Not Elijah, Part 6 (John 9:6-15, 2 Kings 5:10-15) · 2009-11-23

passages.expected_base: And they asked him, What then? Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No.
passages.rationale:
Why the Baptist denies being Elijah in this Gospel
Manning proposes that John assigns several Elijah-Elisha echoes to Jesus while concentrating the Baptist's role on testimony.

«I am not» attracts attention because other Gospels connect the Baptist with Elijah. The usual explanation distinguishes literal identity from prophetic role. Manning additionally proposes a Johannine narrative purpose: the Baptist declines titles and directs toward Jesus attention that might otherwise center on himself.

John omits some Synoptic details resembling Elijah, including the clothing description, while portraying Jesus' signs through parallels with Elijah and Elisha: water requested from a foreign woman, a son's life and multiplied loaves. Manning reads this pattern as emphasizing Jesus' identity, not disparaging the Baptist, whom God sends as a witness (1:6–8).

He also suggests followers retaining allegiance to the Baptist, comparable to Acts 19, as a possible background. That historical reconstruction and the intention assigned to omissions remain hypotheses; a single omission cannot prove them. The explicit point stands: the witness must not take the place of the one he announces.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · I am Not Elijah, Intro · 2009-11-29

passages.expected_base: Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.
passages.rationale:
Thanksgiving that prepares the witnesses' faith
Manning proposes an echo of Psalm 118 to explain the prayer before Lazarus' tomb.

Jesus thanks the Father for hearing him before calling Lazarus out. The next verse explains that he speaks for those present, so they may believe the Father sent him. The prayer discloses a relationship and directs interpretation of the sign rather than informing God of something unknown.

Manning compares the thanksgiving with Psalm 118:21. The psalm celebrates deliverance and declares «I shall not die, but live» (118:17). It also supplies words for Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13) and the rejected cornerstone. This network makes the proposed parallel pertinent to life restored.

The Greek verbs for thanking and hearing differ, so this is an argued allusion rather than an exact quotation. Manning also suggests wordplays involving Jesus' and Lazarus' names, explicitly treating them as more speculative. The main explanation does not depend on them: the witnesses are to recognize the giver of life and the Father who sent Jesus.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jesus' Prayer for Lazarus (John 11) · 2009-07-29
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/07/jesus-prayer-for-lazarus-john-11.html

passages.expected_base: And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant.
passages.rationale:
Naaman's confession frames the difficult request that follows
Acknowledgment of Israel's God prepares a real tension between new allegiance and duties in a foreign court.

After healing, Naaman does more than thank the prophet: he declares that there is no God except in Israel. Manning follows the scene into 5:17–19. The commander requests earth, promises not to sacrifice to other gods and asks forgiveness for accompanying his king when he bows in Rimmon's temple.

The earth probably serves a place of worship to the Lord in Naaman's homeland. His pledge excludes merely adding Israel's God to a collection of equal deities. The difficulty is whether bowing while supporting the king itself constitutes worship. Manning distinguishes assisting the monarch physically from offering the devotion Naaman has just renounced.

«Go in peace» thus welcomes a newly converted foreigner rather than authorizing idolatry generally. Manning acknowledges tension with texts opposing bowing before images. The narrative requires examining the act's purpose and function without dissolving the exclusive allegiance expressed in its opening confession.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Grace to Naaman (2 Kings 5) · 2009-06-22

passages.note_title: Naaman's confession frames the difficult request that follows
passages.note_lead: Acknowledgment of Israel's God prepares a real tension between new allegiance and duties in a foreign court.
passages.note_body:
After healing, Naaman does more than thank the prophet: he declares that there is no God except in Israel. Manning follows the scene into 5:17–19. The commander requests earth, promises not to sacrifice to other gods and asks forgiveness for accompanying his king when he bows in Rimmon's temple.

The earth probably serves a place of worship to the Lord in Naaman's homeland. His pledge excludes merely adding Israel's God to a collection of equal deities. The difficulty is whether bowing while supporting the king itself constitutes worship. Manning distinguishes assisting the monarch physically from offering the devotion Naaman has just renounced.

«Go in peace» thus welcomes a newly converted foreigner rather than authorizing idolatry generally. Manning acknowledges tension with texts opposing bowing before images. The narrative requires examining the act's purpose and function without dissolving the exclusive allegiance expressed in its opening confession.

passages.expected_base: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
passages.rationale:
«One another» makes love a shared practice
Manning gathers reciprocal New Testament commands to show the concrete shape of community life.

Jesus does not simply prescribe a religious feeling. Loving «one another» identifies a relationship among disciples and makes his own love their measure. Footwashing in the same chapter provides a concrete act of service; verse 35 connects such love with public recognition of his followers.

Manning groups other reciprocal commands: carrying burdens (Galatians 6:2), forgiving (Ephesians 4:32), teaching and admonishing (Colossians 3:16), offering hospitality (1 Peter 4:9) and encouraging (1 Thessalonians 5:11). He also gathers warnings against lying, envy and destructive speech toward one another.

His contribution is a thematic collection, rather than a new technical definition of love. The command unfolds in mutual attention, humble correction and practical help. Reciprocity prevents reducing the community to a leader who gives everything and passive recipients: every disciple participates in caring for others according to Jesus' example.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The One Anothers · 2009-06-09

passages.expected_base: Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Eben–ezer, saying, Hitherto hath the Lord helped us.
passages.rationale:
Ebenezer: what changed between defeat and victory
The stone remembers God's help; the narrative explains why bringing the ark had not secured it.

In 1 Samuel 4, Israel loses a battle and brings the ark into camp, expecting its presence to secure victory. Instead, Israel suffers another defeat and the Philistines capture the ark. Its accompanying priests, Hophni and Phinehas, had already been condemned for abusing sacrifices and the women serving at the sanctuary (2:12–25). Possessing the symbol of God's presence does not make their conduct faithful.

Chapter 7 presents a different response. The people remove their idols, fast and confess their sin; Samuel intercedes and offers a sacrifice (7:3–10). The Lord intervenes for them. Afterward, Samuel erects Ebenezer, a «stone of help», to commemorate help received, rather than to produce another victory.

Manning observes that both episodes involve religious practices. The difference is the repentance expressed in the second. He applies this distinction to worship, baptism, communion and fasting: performing them does not obligate God to bless; they should express lives actually turning toward him.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Victory at Ebenezer (1 Samuel 4-7) · 2009-05-07

passages.expected_base: Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.
passages.rationale:
Blindness does not establish a hidden guilt to discover
Manning compares two Johannine healings to show why suffering cannot receive one uniform explanation.

The disciples ask who sinned so that the man was born blind: he or his parents. Jesus rejects that alternative and directs attention to God's works being revealed. The narrative does not authorize searching for concealed wrongdoing in every sick person.

Manning compares John 5 and 9. Both concern prolonged disability, healing near a Jerusalem pool on a Sabbath and subsequent controversy. Responses differ: the man in John 5 informs the authorities about Jesus; the man in John 9 defends him, endures expulsion and comes to faith. Jesus warns the first about sin while rejecting the blame-based explanation proposed for the second.

These differences prevent turning one particular warning into a universal rule. John portrays Jesus as giving life, light and care amid rejection. The comparison does not answer every question about suffering; it clarifies that this blindness should not be read as evidence of personal or inherited guilt.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Blind and Lame (John 5, John 9) · 2009-04-20
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/04/blind-and-lame-john-5-and-9.html

passages.expected_base: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.
passages.rationale:
A new tomb and the limits of reconstructing its details
Manning relates burial to known practices, but comparisons cannot identify this tomb's exact stone or textiles.

John emphasizes the garden's proximity and an unused tomb, suitable for burial before the Sabbath (19:42). Other Gospels add a stone closing the entrance. Manning explains how some affluent family tombs used movable stones, sometimes circular and seated in a channel, making closure easier than reopening.

That arrangement helps explain the women's concern about moving a large stone. Sizes and weights calculated from other tombs are not measurements of Jesus' own stone and should not become exact facts supposedly supplied by this verse.

Manning also discusses a Jerusalem discovery of burial textiles with separate head and body pieces, comparable to John 20:5–7. Archaeology supplies context for such practices rather than identifying Jesus' particular cloths. It illuminates historical burial without confidently completing details John does not provide.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · The Rolling Stone · 2009-04-13

passages.expected_base: Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can.
passages.rationale:
The tomb guard within Roman government
Manning favors a detachment from Pilate and explains official concern about a tomb during Passover.

The leaders request a secured tomb to prevent removal of the body and a resurrection claim. Pilate's reply can be understood as «you have a guard» or «take a guard». The isolated expression leaves room to debate whether it refers to personnel already available or grants the governor's soldiers.

Manning favors the latter. He places the request in a heavily watched Passover Jerusalem, where messianic expectations could provoke unrest. The continuation also matters: soldiers report to the priests, who promise to intervene if the matter reaches the governor (28:11–15). This relationship with Pilate supports his identification of troops under Roman authority.

«Roman» need not mean every soldier was born in Rome: Manning distinguishes the governor's forces, regional auxiliaries and high-priestly officers. The historical proposal explains participants and interests without making the initial wording grammatically unambiguous or supplying an exact guard number Matthew does not give.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Soldiers in the Gospels · 2026-04-27

passages.expected_base: He saith unto them, Come and see. They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was about the tenth hour.
passages.rationale:
Coming, seeing and staying: how following begins
Manning observes a chain of action and testimony before the disciples have witnessed Jesus' signs.

Two disciples hear the Baptist point to Jesus and follow him. Asking where he stays, they receive an invitation to come and see, then spend the day with him. Their relationship begins through approach and companionship rather than complete understanding of everything they will later learn.

Manning highlights repeated words in 1:19–51: seeking, finding, seeing and following. Andrew finds Peter and shares his recognition; Philip does something similar with Nathanael. One person's testimony leads another toward a firsthand encounter. Their titles express true but still partial understanding of Jesus.

Possible Elijah-Elisha echoes are secondary and less certain than this visible pattern. Nor must every verb for seeing encode a different spiritual level: John also varies synonyms. Discipleship begins in trust responding to testimony, continues in remaining with Jesus and becomes testimony offered to others.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Jesus' First Disciples in John (John 1:19-51) · 2009-02-02
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2009/02/jesus-first-disciples-in-john.html
passages.editorial_audit: Repeated seeing and following structure the calling. Do not assign fixed theological distinctions to every synonym for seeing.

One person's testimony leads another toward a firsthand encounter. Their titles express true but still partial understanding of Jesus.

Possible Elijah-Elisha echoes are secondary and less certain than this visible pattern. Nor must every verb for seeing encode a different spiritual level: John also varies synonyms. Discipleship begins in trust responding to testimony, continues in remaining with Jesus and becomes testimony offered to others.

passages.expected_base: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
passages.rationale:
Joy for the people opens a story reaching the nations
Manning places the shepherds' announcement within Israel's hope and the later development of Luke and Acts.

«All people» can sound immediately universal without distinction. Manning observes that laos here refers to Israel. The announcement occurs in David's city and identifies the newborn as Savior, Messiah and Lord, answering hopes already expressed in the songs of Luke 1–2.

Mary celebrates God her Savior; Zechariah speaks of redemption, forgiveness and fearless service; Simeon recognizes salvation he has seen. This repetition makes Luke's nativity more than a tender scene. It announces deliverance from sin and a life directed toward God.

The initial emphasis on Israel does not exclude other nations. Simeon also speaks of light for Gentiles (2:32), and the narrative develops that perspective through the mission in Acts. The distinction preserves the story's movement: promise fulfilled in Israel and salvation extending to the nations without erasing the announcement's first audience.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Salvation in Luke's Christmas (Luke 1, Luke 2) · 2008-12-12

passages.expected_base: And he charged them that they should tell no man: but the more he charged them, so much the more a great deal they published it;
passages.rationale:
Why healing can be followed by a command to silence
Manning offers several possible reasons for Jesus' reserve and notes that Mark supplies no single explanation here.

After healing the deaf man with a speech difficulty, Jesus orders silence, yet the news spreads further. The instruction surprises readers because the benefit seems worth announcing. Manning places it alongside Mark's other secrecy commands without assuming one motive explains them all.

He proposes three considerations. A reputation as healer could obstruct travel: after another healing became public, Jesus could no longer enter towns openly (1:45). Publicity might also detach miracles from the kingdom and repentance, reducing him to a wonder-worker. Finally, in 1:44 Jesus requests priestly verification; Manning suggests verified testimony may matter more than rumor.

That last explanation directly concerns the leper and applies only by analogy elsewhere. More broadly, disciples must understand messiahship through cross and resurrection. These are plausible reasons for exploring secrecy, rather than a motive expressly detailed in 7:36 or a universal prohibition of testimony.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Mark's Secrecy (Mark 7:36) · 2008-06-12

passages.expected_base: Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts.
passages.rationale:
The king must remember those others try to forget
Manning places the distressed person's drink within Lemuel's responsibility to govern justly.

Read alone, the verse appears to recommend making sufferers drunk so they forget poverty. Lemuel's mother has just warned that kings must not drink until they forget decrees and pervert the afflicted person's rights (31:4–5). She subsequently commands defense of poor and needy people (31:8–9).

Manning reads 31:6–7 as a contrast: someone in misery seeks forgetfulness, while a resourceful king must remember obligations to those people. His drunkenness cannot remedy injustice and may worsen it through neglect. This connects the difficult saying with the paragraph's concern for responsible government.

He also considers sharing wine as a gift with the needy rather than reserving it for royal luxury. Both readings depend on context, rather than making intoxication a general relief policy. The contribution explains a warning about justice; the proverb is not an isolated instruction for treating suffering with alcohol.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · A Toast to Lemuel's Mother · 2008-03-13
https://eutychusnerd.blogspot.com/2008/03/toast-to-lemuels-mother.html

passages.expected_base: And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him.
passages.rationale:
Eutychus lives and the community receives comfort
Manning reads the accident through Acts' themes of teaching, shared meals, God's power and care for established churches.

Eutychus falls from the third floor during the extended meeting and is taken up dead (20:9). Paul descends, embraces him and announces that life is in him. The ending describes the young man alive and the believers comforted (20:12). Paul's announcement need not negate the narrator's preceding description.

Manning compares Troas with Acts 2:42–47: apostolic teaching, shared food, fellowship and divine power. The episode is more than a humorous warning against lengthy preaching or sleeping listeners. The young man's recovery gives real comfort to a community preparing to farewell the apostle.

He also places it within Paul's service to established churches: encouragement in Macedonia, comfort in Troas and exhortation to Ephesian elders. Related language of encouragement links the actions. Mission involves strengthening and caring for existing believers as well as founding new communities.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Eutychus · 2008-03-03

passages.expected_base: And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.
passages.rationale:
The risen Jesus explains the mission through Scripture
Manning groups post-resurrection teaching around Jesus' death and life, the commissioned community and hope of his return.

Jesus recalls the fulfillment of what was written in Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms. The explanation continues with suffering, resurrection and proclamation of repentance for forgiveness to all nations (24:46–47). Scripture provides a framework for events and the witnesses' task rather than a collection of secret codes.

Manning compares the appearance summaries: disciples receive evidence of resurrection, a commission, the Spirit's promise and renewed responsibilities. Acts 1 adds kingdom teaching and a warning that its times are not theirs to determine. These themes develop what Jesus taught before the passion.

Preserved summaries do not authorize reconstructing unrecorded speeches or inventing a different hidden doctrinal program. They disclose a clear movement: understanding Jesus, receiving power to testify and living as a commissioned community. The opening of Scripture leads into that mission.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · What did Jesus Teach After the Resurrection? · 2008-03-20

passages.expected_base: And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
passages.rationale:
Jesus' promise does not depend on a prayer formula
Manning distinguishes faith and repentance expressed in the encounter from a verbal ritual supposedly producing salvation.

The condemned man acknowledges guilt, declares Jesus innocent and asks remembrance in his kingdom (23:40–42). Jesus answers with the promise of paradise. No standardized prayer or instruction to repeat prescribed words appears.

Manning uses this case to address the «sinner's prayer». Prayer can sincerely express repentance and trust in Christ; the problem comes when reciting a formula is taught to guarantee salvation itself. The man's response matters through its orientation toward Jesus, rather than conformity to a later devotional script.

The contribution does not substitute another formula or use crucifixion's exceptional circumstances to make discipleship irrelevant. Manning notes that Acts connects faith, when possible, with baptism and entry into community. This scene shows Jesus' saving initiative in an extreme situation without making a modern evangelistic method a requirement Luke never states.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Sinner's Prayer · 2009-02-06

Manning uses this case to address the «sinner's prayer». Prayer can sincerely express repentance and trust in Christ; the problem comes when reciting a formula is taught to guarantee salvation itself. The man's response matters through its orientation toward Jesus, rather than conformity to a later devotional script.

The contribution does not substitute another formula or use crucifixion's exceptional circumstances to make discipleship irrelevant. Manning notes that Acts connects faith, when possible, with baptism and entry into community. This scene shows Jesus' saving initiative in an extreme situation without making a modern evangelistic method a requirement Luke never states.

passages.expected_base: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
passages.rationale:
The warning includes coming wrath, not merely insincerity
Manning shows how a paraphrase can preserve the Baptist's severity while losing a central part of his message.

The Baptist's question does more than rebuke those approaching baptism: it names flight from coming wrath. Following verses require fruit of repentance and develop judgment through the axe and fire (3:8–12).

Comparing the Greek with The Message, Manning observes that the paraphrase stresses the inadequacy of entering the river without change. It can convey suspected hypocrisy while omitting the explicit future wrath. A vivid account of motive does not necessarily preserve everything the original says.

The contribution identifies what a translation must retain: repentance's demand and judgment's horizon together. This does not require reproducing Greek order at all costs; clear translation can rearrange a sentence. It should not replace part of its content with an interpretation readers can no longer distinguish from the Baptist's own warning.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Problem Passages in The Message · 2016-11-29
https://www.biola.edu/blogs/good-book-blog/2016/problem-passages-in-the-message

passages.expected_base: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.
passages.rationale:
Promised reward is more than present approval
Manning distinguishes the hope sustaining persecuted disciples from a paraphrase that changes the promise's content.

Jesus calls those slandered and persecuted for his sake to rejoice. The stated reason is a great reward in heaven, together with continuity with persecuted prophets. The sentence looks beyond the immediate judgment of those opposing the disciples.

Manning compares this with The Message's image of present heavenly approval. That may be evocative, but it does not fully convey the promised reward. The paraphrase also explains persecutors psychologically, as uncomfortable with the truth; the Greek text supplies no such explanation here.

This distinction protects two features: hope does not depend on receiving recognition now, and readers should not attribute an added explanation of every opponent to Jesus. Commentary may explore applications; translation should leave the promise and its basis recognizable without confusing them with an interpreter's expansion.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Problem Passages in The Message · 2016-11-29

passages.expected_base: And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
passages.rationale:
The concern is provision, not fashion
Manning warns that turning clothing into vanity can conceal the material need Jesus addresses.

The lilies belong to teaching about eating, drinking and clothing (6:25–34). Obtaining these necessities could be urgent for Jesus' hearers. He speaks of trust in the Father and the kingdom's priority rather than assuming that concern arises from luxury-seeking.

Manning observes that The Message recasts clothing through fashion, appearance and shopping. The image may connect readily with modern readers but moves the issue from fear of lacking necessities to concern about looking better. This obscures part of the comfort addressed to vulnerable people.

Lilies do not spin, yet receive beauty surpassing Solomon's. The comparison points toward God's care for his creatures. Translation should preserve the relationship between need, provision and trust; applications to consumption can then be considered separately. One application should not displace the concrete question of daily life.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Problem Passages in The Message · 2016-11-29

passages.expected_base: But he saith unto them, It is I; be not afraid.
passages.rationale:
«It is I»: identification with a possible divine resonance
Manning recognizes Jesus identifying himself while suggesting that walking on the sea adds a larger scriptural background.

The disciples are frightened when Jesus approaches on the water. «It is I; be not afraid» tells them who is coming. Egō eimi is ordinary self-identification; it is not invariably a divine name, as the healed man's words in John 9:9 demonstrate.

Manning nevertheless finds an additional resonance plausible here. Job 9:8 describes God walking upon the sea in Greek wording close to John 6:19. The action on the waters, identification and reassurance together lead him to read a manifestation of divine identity.

The argument rests on that combination rather than making two ordinary words an automatic code. Translation can retain natural self-identification while commentary explains the proposed background. This neither erases a possible allusion nor makes every Greek speaker saying «I am» claim to be God.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Does "I Am" always refer to God in the Gospel of John? · 2015-09-21

passages.expected_base: Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
passages.rationale:
«Before Abraham was»: context gives weight to «I am»
The claim to existence before Abraham distinguishes this occurrence from ordinary self-identification.

Manning rejects treating egō eimi as invariably exclusive to God. The New Testament also gives it to Peter, Paul and the healed man in John 9. The significance of 8:58 therefore cannot be demonstrated by isolating those two words.

Here the conversation concerns Abraham and Jesus' identity. His hearers contrast his apparent age with seeing the patriarch (8:57). Jesus places his existence before Abraham and uses «I am» without another predicate. Their attempt to stone him shows that they do not receive the statement as a trivial observation about age.

Manning finds preexistence and divine resonance in this combination. His reading does not require denying the same expression's ordinary uses elsewhere. Comparing them helps identify what makes this declaration distinctive: its speaker, the question being answered and the claim about Abraham's time.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Does "I Am" always refer to God in the Gospel of John? · 2015-09-21

passages.expected_base: Some said, This is he: others said, He is like him: but he said, I am he.
passages.rationale:
«I am» can simply mean «I am the one»
The healed man's answer tests any claim that the Greek expression always carries divine meaning.

Neighbors debate whether the man who now sees is the former beggar. He settles the question by identifying himself: «I am he». The Greek is egō eimi, the same expression found in several sayings of Jesus. Here it asserts personal identity rather than claiming a divine title.

Manning uses this example to show that the words alone are not a code for God's name. Extraordinary significance elsewhere must be argued from context: Jesus' claim concerning Abraham in 8:58 or his action on the sea in 6:19–20, rather than merely locating the same two words.

The distinction strengthens the method of interpreting John's christology. It also preserves the healed man's voice as he describes his experience and answers those debating who he is. Natural self-identification communicates that response without imposing a significance the scene does not require.

Source: Gary Manning Jr. · Does "I Am" always refer to God in the Gospel of John? · 2015-09-21
